# tabnas — full text for language models

> tabnas is an extensible parsing engine and a compile target for agents. A
> grammar is data — a table of rules and token alternates the engine walks at
> runtime — so a new language is usually rules added to one that already
> parses, rather than a new parser. Because that data is flat and declarative,
> a language model can emit a grammar directly, and you can check it before
> running it. Implemented in TypeScript and Go. Open source (MIT), sponsored
> by Voxgig. Site: https://tabnas.dev

## What tabnas is

A grammar is not turned into generated code — the grammar *is* the parser, a
table the engine walks. Install a grammar package, compile ABNF at runtime, or
write the table directly. Because it stays data, you can inspect a live
grammar, render it back to ABNF, or draw it as a railroad diagram.

Two consequences, and they are why the project exists:

1. **Extension is cheap.** JSONC is JSON with comments; jsonic is JSONC with
   the quoting relaxed. You add rules to a grammar that already parses rather
   than forking a parser.
2. **The engine is a good compile target.** ABNF compiles into it, for humans.
   And the rule table is flat declarative data with no control flow, which is a
   shape a model can emit reliably.

"tabnas" is Irish — *Tábla na nAistrithe*, "a table of translations."

## Quickstart (TypeScript)

    npm install @tabnas/parser @tabnas/abnf

Define a grammar in ABNF and parse:

    import { Tabnas } from '@tabnas/parser'
    import { abnf } from '@tabnas/abnf'

    const tn = new Tabnas({ plugins: [abnf] })
    tn.abnf(`
      val = add
      add = NR [ PL add ]
      PL  = "+"
    `)

    tn.parse('1+2+3')
    // => { rule: 'val', src: '1+2+3', kids: [ ... ] }

`NR` is the built-in number token; `[ ... ]` is optional; a rule may refer to
itself. The Go path mirrors this via `github.com/tabnas/parser/go`.

Recognising is not computing. To get a value, attach actions by reference:

    tn.abnf(GRAMMAR, {
      actions: {
        // `val` holds the running total.
        '@val:o:add': (r) => { r.node.value = 0 },
        // Each number adds to it.
        '@add:o:NR': (r) => { r.parent.node.value += r.o[0].val },
      },
    })

    tn.parse('1+2+3').value   // => 6

Both names are alternate marks. `r.parent` is `val` for every repetition,
because a tail self-reference (`[ PL add ]`) compiles to a same-depth repeat
of the rule — the same `{ s: '#PL', r: 'add' }` close alternate a
hand-written rule table declares. Keep results on the node rather than in a
variable outside the parse, so the grammar stays reusable. Mark names are
assigned by the compiler — list them with
`tabnas-abnf --marks -f grammar.abnf` rather than guessing.

## The rule table

The grammar format, which is what an agent should emit:

    {
      options: {
        fixed: { token: { '#PL': '+' } },
        rule:  { start: 'val' },
      },
      rule: {
        val: { open: [ { p: 'add' } ], close: [ {} ] },
        add: {
          open:  [ { s: '#NR' } ],
          close: [ { s: '#PL', r: 'add' }, {} ],
        },
      },
    }

Alternate fields: `s` matches a token sequence (its length sets this
alternate's lookahead depth); `p` pushes a child rule; `r` repeats a rule at
the same stack depth; `a` is an action; `c` a condition; `{}` is the empty
alternate that ends a phase.

`p` versus `r` matters: push nests, so the child's parent is the pushing rule;
repeat stays flat, so every repetition shares one parent — which is what makes
an accumulator a single value in one place.

Engine `$`-builtin actions are referenced by name, so a grammar can be pure
JSON with no functions in it: `@object$`, `@array$`, `@key$`, `@setval$`,
`@push$`, `@value$`, `@reset$` (native values), and `@node$`, `@capture$`,
`@bubble$` (tree building).

    { "rule": { "val": {
      "open":  [ { "s": "#NR", "a": "@value$" } ],
      "close": [ {} ]
    } } }
    // tn.parse('42')  =>  42

## The syntax tree

Every parse through the ABNF compiler yields the same shape:

    { rule: string, src: string, kids: Node[] }

so walkers, actions, and tooling written once apply to every grammar.

## Constraints

- Deterministic: alternates are tried in order, first match wins.
- No backtracking, and no ambiguity — one parse per input, or an error.
- Lookahead depth is declared by each alternate; there is no fixed ceiling.
- You write the lexer. tabnas separates lexing from parsing and is mostly about
  the parsing half; built-in tokens and fixed tokens cover a lot.
- ABNF desugars `[ ... ]` and `( ... )` into generated group rules, so at
  runtime a rule's `parent` is often synthetic rather than the rule above it in
  your source.

## ABNF notes

- RFC 5234 dialect: `=` and `/` (not `::=`).
- Built-in tokens by bareword: `NR` (number), plus core rules like `ALPHA`,
  `DIGIT`.
- Left recursion is accepted and rewritten (Paull's algorithm): `P = P a / b`
  becomes `P = b *(a)`. The tree comes out flat rather than left-nested, and a
  purely left-recursive rule (no base branch) is an error.

## Packages

25 in total (npm `@tabnas/<name>`, Go `github.com/tabnas/<name>/go`). Full list
with current versions: https://tabnas.dev/releases

- Engine: parser
- Grammar tooling: abnf, debug, railroad
- Languages and formats: json, jsonc, json5, jsonic, yaml, toml, ini, csv, xml,
  markdown, css, c, proto, zon, feed
- Syntax plugins: expr, directive, hoover, path, multisource
- Command line: jsonic-cli

Everything is pre-1.0 — pin exact versions.

## For agents

- Check whether an existing grammar parses something close to your format and
  extend it before writing anything. That is the mechanism the engine exists
  for, and the cheapest path.
- Prefer emitting a rule table with `$`-builtin actions: it stays pure JSON,
  which is checkable and serialisable.
- Every package repository ships an `AGENTS.md`.
- Every package ships tested, runnable README examples (`// =>` assertions are
  executed in CI).
- Build guide for agents: https://tabnas.dev/agents
- Machine-readable index: https://tabnas.dev/llms.txt

## Real languages built on tabnas

- aontu (TypeScript) — a CUE-like JSON structure unifier, assembled from the
  jsonic, expr, directive, multisource, path and debug plugins with no parser
  of its own. https://github.com/rjrodger/aontu
- boru (Go) — a typed, word-based query language with parser, type checker,
  formatter and LSP, built on parser, jsonic, abnf, csv and expr.
  https://github.com/boru-lang/boru
- chess (TypeScript, ported to Go) — PGN and SAN chess notation, a grammar
  plugin on the bare engine. The board on https://tabnas.dev/examples plays
  a game through it. The plugin parses notation only; resolving `Nf3` to a
  particular knight needs the position, so the board view supplies its own
  legal move generator. https://github.com/tabnas/chess

## How-to guides

Task-oriented pages at https://tabnas.dev/how-to, each solving one problem
against a running grammar. Every sample is executed before it ships.

Composing grammars:

- Include one source from another — the `@` mark, resolvers, processors,
  dependency tracking, and the `@tabnas/directive` mechanism underneath.
  https://tabnas.dev/how-to/include-other-sources
- Parse expressions with precedence — `@tabnas/expr`, the binding-power scale,
  custom operators, function-call syntax, evaluation.
  https://tabnas.dev/how-to/expressions-with-precedence
- Write a parameterised parser — plugin `defaults`, deep-merged options, and
  the five things an option can change (token, lexer, IGNORE set, rule groups,
  the parser itself). https://tabnas.dev/how-to/parameterised-parsers

Shaping the parse:

- Handle recursion and repetition — `r` versus `p`, tail self-reference, the
  ABNF left-recursion rewrite, and depth guards.
  https://tabnas.dev/how-to/recursion-and-repetition
- Choose between alternates — order, multi-token lookahead, `c`, counters, `b`,
  and group tags. https://tabnas.dev/how-to/choose-between-alternates
- Parse a line-oriented format — taking `#LN` out of the IGNORE set; a worked
  INI grammar; `@tabnas/csv`. https://tabnas.dev/how-to/line-oriented-formats

Feeding the lexer:

- Lex a token the engine doesn't know — `fixed.token`, `match.token`,
  `match.value`, and a hand-written matcher.
  https://tabnas.dev/how-to/custom-tokens
- Handle comments and whitespace — comment definitions, `eatline`, and what
  `IGNORE` costs. https://tabnas.dev/how-to/comments-and-whitespace
- Handle strings, quotes and escapes — quote characters, multi-line strings,
  escape tables, CSV-style doubling.
  https://tabnas.dev/how-to/strings-and-quoting

Working on a grammar:

- Debug a grammar — `rule()`, `sub()`, `@tabnas/debug` describe/model/trace,
  `@tabnas/railroad`. https://tabnas.dev/how-to/debug-a-grammar
- Give good parse errors — `fileName`, `errmsg.name`, custom codes with
  `{brace}` injection, the `e` alternate, `token.bad()`.
  https://tabnas.dev/how-to/parse-errors
- Test a grammar — fresh instances, accept/reject tables, asserting on
  `e.code`, ABNF round-trip, `tabnas-abnf --parse`.
  https://tabnas.dev/how-to/test-a-grammar
